newsitem.title: CHINA: Korean banks down but not out - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Korean banks down but not out - analysts.

text.p: Problems in the corporate and banking sectors of South Korea are dire, but the danger of a Thai-style meltdown in the financial sector of Korea is remote, analysts told Reuters Financial Television on Wednesday.
A recent spate of defaults by high profile Korean firms has heightened the risks faced by South Korean banks.

"The Korean banking system has had fundamental problems for quite some time," Chris Francis, Director and Head of Fixed Income Research at Merrill Lynch in Hong Kong told Reuters Financial Television on the daily market show "Asia Today".
Francis said low core profitability and weak capital ratios were among factors combining with the current credit crunch in the corporate sector to create a serious threat to Korean banks.

"I think you can say this is a problem for the whole banking system not just an isolated problem for a particular institution," said Francis, "I think there's a challenge for the government in actually keeping this whole system on course."
But while most analysts agree the problems in the banking sector are serious, few think there is a risk that the banks of "Korea Inc", with the sovereign support of the Bank of Korea, will default.

"Investors should be aware that sure there are fundamental sensitivities with the intrinsic quality of the banks," said John Woods, Head of Research at HSBC Markets in Hong Kong, "but in terms of the support by the government, that hasn't changed."

At the height of the Thai financial crisis precipitated by the "managed float" of the currency, investors in longer term US dollar denominated Thai debt were jarred by reports that government officials were suggesting that Thai corporates facing liquidity problems should default on their off-shore obligations before failing to meet local demands.
Woods says such a scenario is far less likely to occur in South Korea, where banks have borrowed extensively in the off-shore market, raising billions of dollars annually.
"The Government is clearly aware that foreign investment - an inward source of funding - is crucial to its development," said Woods.

Merrill Lynch's Francis agrees. "I don't think there's any issue that the financial system can't fund itself," he said, "but it's a case of what's the price of funding itself and what maturity of what debt can it raise."
Even the troubled corporates are expected to be supported by the government, if not directly.
"I think the government policy has been very consistent," said Steve Xu, Treasury Economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Hong Kong.

"The top 30 Chaebol (conglomerates) are not going to go under, I mean Kia is not going to go under, it is going to be protected - the same goes for Hanbo, because the consequence to subcontractors and suppliers is just too grave," he said.
Analysts say there are other key factors that differentiate South Korea from Thailand.
Unlike the Thai baht at the outset of that country's financial crisis, the Korean won is not freely tradable in international markets.
The "closed" nature of South Korea's capital account makes it all but impossible for hedge funds to speculate on the currency.
Another factor is the underlying health of the Korean economy.
In the early part of 1997, South Korea saw the won fall from 840 won to the US dollar, all the way to 890 by the end of June.

This competitive devaluation started to pay off when the Japanese yen firmed down to around 110 to the US dollar, making Korean goods competing with Japanese exports far cheaper in international markets.
The weakness of the won and a gradual economic upturn for South Korea is widely seen helping take some of the sting out of the current wave of corporate credit crunches.
